issues.item: Compulsive Exercise: I push myself to exercise excessively
issues.explanation: The maladaptive strategies cluster is not well anchored to the rest of the profile. Excessive exercise and alcohol use can occur in PTSD, but in this profile they are hard to connect to the dominant threat-memory pattern centered on danger vigilance after a motor vehicle collision. With no trigger links active, these strategies should still fit the patient’s central formulation via memory/threat/appraisals, yet these two items feel relatively generic and not clearly tied to the reported intrusive reliving, vigilance, and environmental scanning.

Dehumanization is the main inconsistent appraisal. Feeling like an object is more characteristic of interpersonal trauma involving humiliation, coercion, or abuse than a life-threatening motor vehicle collision. It also sits awkwardly beside the rest of the profile, which is strongly organized around danger anticipation, distrust, and reliving of the crash. In contrast, shame on recall plus dehumanization suggests a different trauma meaning that is not otherwise represented in the memory, threat, or strategy items.

issues.item: Shame on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense shame
issues.explanation: For a life-threatening motor vehicle collision, intense shame on recall is not impossible, but in this profile it is weakly supported by the rest of the content. The other memory items emphasize sensory reliving and replay, while no appraisal item directly explains shame about the event (e.g. self-blame, humiliation, permanent damage). This makes the shame item clinically hard to integrate with the rest of the profile.

issues.item: Dehumanization: I feel like an object, not like a person
issues.explanation: 'I feel like an object, not like a person' is more characteristic of interpersonal trauma, coercion, or dehumanizing abuse than a motor vehicle collision. In this profile there are no companion items about bodily violation, humiliation, or identity damage that would make this appraisal cohere after an MVC.

issues.item: Distrust Others: People are not what they seem
issues.explanation: 'People are not what they seem' implies a generalized interpersonal mistrust. For an MVC profile dominated by danger scanning and reliving, that belief is possible but is not well anchored by the trauma type or by other selected items, which focus on environmental threat rather than betrayal or intentional human threat. This creates a cross-node mismatch in the formulation content.

issues.item: Seeking Conflict: I pick arguments or create drama to distract myself from the trauma
issues.explanation: This item is the main coherence problem. For a 24-year-old female survivor of a life-threatening motor vehicle collision, the rest of the profile is tightly organized around fear-based PTSD: hypervigilant threat monitoring, danger-focused appraisals, and highly sensory reliving memory. 'Seeking Conflict' reflects an externalizing/drama-generating coping style that is not supported by the other selected items and does not fit the predominant cognitive formulation as well as the other strategies do. Alcohol use and checking surroundings plausibly connect to threat and memory, but picking arguments to distract herself pulls toward a different presentation and is hard to explain from the rest of the profile.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Alcohol Use: drink alcohol
issues.explanation: Alcohol use is not impossible, but in this profile it is weakly integrated with the rest of the selected content. The other items depict a tightly fear-based, hypervigilant motor-vehicle-collision presentation focused on environmental scanning, sleep vigilance, back-to-wall positioning, reliving, and danger-based appraisals. A solitary alcohol-use item without any parallel avoidance/numbing/interpersonal dysregulation content makes the coping pattern feel clinically disconnected from the rest of the formulation.

issues.item: Threat: Noticing Weapons: I notice potential weapons or dangerous objects in any environment
issues.explanation: For a life-threatening motor vehicle collision, generalized scanning for threat is coherent, but specifically 'noticing weapons' pulls toward assault/interpersonal violence content. Given that the rest of the profile is entirely accident-based and contains no interpersonal-threat, attack, or weapon-related memory/appraisal material, this item is difficult to reconcile with the otherwise coherent accident formulation.

vignette:
Lena Haddad is a twenty-four-year-old Lebanese-American woman who works as a tailor from a small alterations shop she rents in a strip mall on the outskirts of her city. She lives alone, is currently single, and presented for psychological assessment approximately eight months after a life-threatening motor vehicle collision that left her with a PCL-5 score of 41 and a daily life that has contracted, quietly and steadily, around the fear of what she is now certain can happen at any moment.

The accident occurred on a Tuesday afternoon in early autumn. Lena was a passenger in a friend's sedan travelling on an interstate when a truck drifted lanes without warning and struck them at highway speed. The car spun, struck the guardrail, and came to rest facing oncoming traffic. Lena was conscious throughout - she remembers the sound of the impact, a low metallic tearing, and the sensation of the seatbelt locking hard across her chest as the world rotated. She remembers thinking, with a clarity she still finds disturbing, that she was going to die before anyone who loved her knew where she was. Her friend sustained a broken wrist; Lena was discharged from the emergency department the same evening with soft-tissue injuries. Physically, she recovered within weeks. Psychologically, she has not.

In the months that followed, Lena found that she could not ride in a vehicle without her body treating the experience as a repetition of the collision. She stopped accepting lifts and began walking or taking the bus, and eventually stopped using the bus as well when she realised she was spending every journey gripping the seat and watching other passengers for signs that something was about to go wrong. She now walks to work, a forty-minute round trip she makes regardless of weather, and has not been a passenger in a car since February. Her world has narrowed accordingly.

What anchors the current clinical picture most powerfully is the quality of Lena's memories of the accident. They do not feel like recollections - they feel like events still in progress. When the memory surfaces, which it does without invitation, she experiences the same terror she felt on the interstate: her heart accelerates, her chest tightens across the old seatbelt line, and she is briefly but completely back inside the spinning car. Because the memory arrives with this full physiological force, her nervous system remains in a state of perpetual readiness, as though the crash is always about to happen again. This persistent sense of present threat feeds directly back into the memory itself - the heightened arousal lowers the threshold for intrusion, so that the film, as she describes it, plays more frequently and with greater intensity the more vigilant she becomes.

Lena has come to believe, with a conviction that feels entirely rational to her, that the world is a dangerous place and that ordinary life offers no reliable protection from catastrophe. She does not trust that other drivers, other pedestrians, or other people in general are what they appear to be - the truck driver had seemed, from a distance, to be in full control of his vehicle. This appraisal of pervasive unpredictable threat keeps her nervous system mobilised and sustains the scanning and hypervigilance that now structure her days. At the alterations shop, she positions herself so that her back is against the wall nearest the cutting table, facing the door, and she monitors every customer who enters with an attention that goes well beyond professional courtesy. She has difficulty falling asleep each night because she feels that to do so would be to surrender the alertness she is certain she needs.

To manage what she has come to understand as a necessary vigilance, Lena scans her environment constantly and mentally rehearses worst-case scenarios - imagining, in detail, what she would do if a car mounted the pavement outside the shop, or if a customer became threatening. She experiences this rehearsal as preparation rather than symptom. Yet the scanning and rehearsal keep the threat schema active, which in turn makes the intrusive memories more accessible, and the memories, arriving with their original terror intact, confirm to Lena that her vigilance is not excessive but essential. The loop has tightened over eight months into something she can no longer manage alone.

What finally brought Lena to seek help was a conversation with her mother, who told her, gently, that she seemed to have disappeared. Lena is most afraid that the fear is permanent. She is most hoping, though she said this quietly and without much conviction, that it does not have to be.
